title: Buddha-nature views
hook: some schools teach inborn Buddha-nature; others speak of what can be developed

segments.voice: Yesterday, one Buddha or many: one teacher on a dusty road, and a sky full of Buddhas. Your line was one and many. What ordinary thing did you see both ways? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

A monk in China comes to the old teacher Zhaozhou with what sounds like an easy question. The sutras say every living being has Buddha-nature. So, does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou answers with one syllable. Wu. No. Nothing. Zen students still sit with that single word, turning it over until something gives. Why would a teacher who knew the sutras say no? Hold on to that. Today, Buddha-nature: whether awakening is something you're born with, something you grow, or both.
screen: `DOES A DOG HAVE BUDDHA-NATURE?` → `WU.` → `BORN, OR GROWN?`

segments.voice: First, the inborn view. A group of Mahayana scriptures, among them the Mahaparinirvana Sutra, teach that all beings have Buddha-nature, sometimes called the tathagatagarbha, the womb or seed of a Buddha. Awakening, in this view, isn't built from scratch. It's already there, covered over like gold in the earth or a jewel sewn into a beggar's coat. Practice uncovers it. Zen, and other schools of East Asia, grew up with this teaching. Second, the koan. If Buddha-nature is already there, why does Zhaozhou say no? Zen teachers say the word isn't a doctrine to agree or disagree with. It's a gate. Holding on to Buddha-nature as an idea can become one more thing to cling to, and Wu cuts the rope. Third, the developmental view. The Theravada speaks less of a hidden Buddha inside and more of qualities to be grown: generosity, ethics, patience, wisdom, the perfections cultivated over a long path. The Pali texts do have a striking line, though. The Anguttara Nikaya says the mind is luminous, and that it is stained by defilements that arrive from outside. Some teachers take that as a seed of the inborn view; others read it simply as a reason to practice. Fourth, voices within one tradition. Tibetan schools debate this too. Some say Buddha-nature is the mind's emptiness, which makes growth possible. Others say it is a radiant nature with qualities already complete. Each explains itself carefully. Born or grown. Some teachers say a practitioner needs both: trust that it's there, and effort to grow it.
screen: `ALL BEINGS HAVE BUDDHA-NATURE.` · `WU: A GATE, NOT A DOCTRINE.` · `QUALITIES TO BE GROWN.` · `THE LUMINOUS MIND.` · then, large: `BORN OR GROWN.`

segments.voice: Here's a way to hear both, if you'd like. Sit and breathe. For the first minute, rest as if there's nothing to add: as if the clear, kind mind is already here, under the noise, like sky behind clouds. Just let the breath show it. For the second minute, choose one quality to grow, patience perhaps, or generosity, and breathe as if you're watering a seed. Don't decide which minute was right. The bell holds the time.
Buddha-nature views. Some schools teach that awakening is already present in every being, waiting to be uncovered; others speak of qualities grown on the path. Today's word.
Your line: born or grown. Today, when you see something good in someone, ask whether it looks born in them or grown by them, and notice you can honor both. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: In Zen, students may work with the koan of Zhaozhou's dog for a long time with a teacher; Theravada practitioners speak of cultivating the perfections, and Tibetan monastic colleges study and debate the nature of Buddha-nature.

fork.setup: you're Zhaozhou. a monk asks: the sutras say every being has Buddha-nature. does a dog? what do you answer?
options: yes, of course; the sutras say so.
fork.reveal: Zhaozhou says Wu. Zen teachers say it isn't a denial of the sutras but a gate to sit with until something gives.

original.note: Sanskrit tathagatagarbha: the womb or seed of the Buddha, one name for Buddha-nature.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddha-nature means everyone is secretly already a Buddha, so nothing needs doing.
what it means: some schools teach awakening is present in all beings, covered over; others stress qualities grown on the path.
what a scholar hears: tathagatagarbha teaching in sutras like the Mahaparinirvana, the luminous mind of the Anguttara, and Tibetan debate over emptiness versus radiant qualities.
